hero.title: Top 5 WhatsApp OTP Mistakes Developers Make (and How to Fix Them)
hero.excerpt: From wrong phone number formats to missing webhook handlers — these are the most common pitfalls developers hit when integrating WhatsApp OTP with Nabda API, and exactly how to fix them.

mistakesPost.intro: WhatsApp OTP integration with Nabda is straightforward — but a few recurring mistakes can cause hours of debugging. Whether you're building a new integration or auditing an existing one, this guide covers the top 5 issues we see in support tickets and how to avoid them.

mistake1.title: Wrong Phone Number Format
mistake1.desc: The most common mistake: sending a phone number without the country code, or with a leading zero instead of the country code. Nabda OTP requires E.164 format — meaning the number must start with a + followed by the country code.
mistake1.tip: Nabda OTP supports all MENA country codes. Iraq: +964, Syria: +963, Egypt: +20, Saudi: +966, UAE: +971. Always validate the format server-side before sending.

mistake2.title: Using the Wrong API Token
mistake2.desc: Nabda OTP has two types of tokens: your global account token and an instance-scoped Bearer token. Sending messages requires the instance token — obtained by calling select-instance. Using your global token will always return 401 Unauthorized.
mistake2.tip: The instance token should be stored securely on your backend and refreshed after each select-instance call. Never expose it in frontend code or logs.

mistake3.title: Storing Plain OTP on the Client
mistake3.desc: Storing an OTP in localStorage, a cookie, or sending it back in the API response is a critical security mistake. Anyone with access to the browser DevTools can see and reuse it. Always generate, hash, and verify OTPs entirely on the backend.
mistake3.tip: Use a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) combined with a server-side secret. Store the hash in your database — never the plain OTP. This way, even a DB leak exposes nothing usable.

mistake4.title: No Expiry or Rate Limiting on OTP Verification
mistake4.desc: An OTP without an expiry time is permanently valid — allowing brute-force attacks. Without rate limiting, an attacker can try all 1,000,000 possible 6-digit codes in minutes. Both protections are essential.
mistake4.tip: Set OTP expiry to 3–8 minutes. Limit verification attempts to 5 per 15-minute window per user. After 5 failed attempts, invalidate the OTP and require a new one.

mistake5.title: Not Monitoring Instance Connection Status
mistake5.desc: A Nabda OTP instance requires a connected WhatsApp session. If the QR code expires or the phone disconnects, your instance goes offline — and OTPs stop delivering silently. Without a webhook, you won't know until users start complaining.
mistake5.tip: Always configure a webhook on your Nabda instance. Listen for instance.disconnected events and alert your team immediately. Consider an automated monitor that checks instance health every few minutes.

checklist.title: Quick Checklist Before Going Live
checklist.c1: Phone numbers use E.164 format with country code (+964, +963, +20…)
checklist.c2: Instance token is fetched via select-instance — not the global account token
checklist.c3: OTPs are hashed server-side, never stored as plain text or sent to the client
checklist.c4: OTP expiry is set (3–8 min) and verification is rate-limited (max 5 attempts)
checklist.c5: Webhook is configured to monitor instance status and message delivery events
